knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, error = TRUE)

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

# Set all plots in this section to have "minima" theme - looks cleaner
theme_set(theme_minimal())
```

## Correlation

A scatterplot shows a downward trend between year and freeze duration in the Lake Monona data.

```{r}
monona <- read_csv("../../data/lake-monona-winters-2025.csv")

ggplot(monona, aes(x = year1, y = duration)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = F)
```

We can calculate correlation with the `cor` function or "by-hand".

```{r}
cor(monona$year1, monona$duration)
cor(monona$duration, monona$year1)
```

```{r}
xbar <- mean(monona$year1)
s_x <- sd(monona$year1)

ybar <- mean(monona$duration)
s_y <- sd(monona$duration)

n <- nrow(monona)

sum((monona$year1 - xbar) * (monona$duration - ybar)) / ((n-1)*s_x*s_y)
```


## Linear modeling

Let's calculate a linear model for the Lake Monona data, and compare to the `lm()` function in R.

```{r}
corr <- cor(monona$year1, monona$duration)
  
est_slope <- corr * (s_y / s_x)

est_intercept <- ybar - est_slope*xbar

est_intercept; est_slope
```

In R, use the syntax `y ~ x` when fitting a model.

```{r}
lake_mod <- lm(duration ~ year1, data = monona)

lake_mod
```


EX 14.1

The dataset `lions.csv` records the age and nose color (what % is black) for 32 individual lions.

```{r}
lions <- read_csv("../../data/lions.csv") %>%
  rename(black = proportion.black)
```

Create a scatterplot of the data, where x = age and y = black.  Does a linear model seem reasonable for this data?

Calculate the least-squares slope and intercept and then check your work with the `lm()` function.


```{r}
lions %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = black)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = F)
```

```{r}
corr <- cor(lions$age, lions$black)

xbar <- mean(lions$age)
s_x <- sd(lions$age)

ybar <- mean(lions$black)
s_y <- sd(lions$black)
```

```{r}
est_slope <- corr * (s_y / s_x)
est_intercept <- ybar - est_slope*xbar

est_slope; est_intercept
```

```{r}
lion_mod <- lm(black ~ age, data = lions)

lion_mod
```

```{r}
# Est. nose color for 5yo lion
0.06970 + 0.05859*5
```




We can also get more information about a linear model by using the `summary()` command.

```{r}
summary(lake_mod)
```


## Model validation

We evaluate the assumptions (i.e., validate the linear model fit) by studying the residuals.  For ease of graphing, we can add the residuals to our data.

```{r}
resid(lake_mod)
predict(lake_mod)

monona_resids <- monona %>% 
  mutate(residuals = resid(lake_mod),
         pred_duration = predict(lake_mod)) %>% 
  select(year1, duration, pred_duration, residuals)
  
monona_resids

monona_resids %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year1, y = residuals)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0)
```


Let's do the same for the lion data.

```{r}
lion_mod <- lm(black ~ age, data = lions)

lions %>%
  mutate(residuals = resid(lion_mod)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = residuals)) +
  geom_point() + geom_hline(yintercept = 0)
```


## Prediction

Linear models are commonly used for prediction.  For example, we predicted the nose color of a 5-year-old lion to be about 36% black.  

```{r}
predict(lion_mod, newdata = tibble(age = 5))
```


EX 14.2

Using `lion_mod` and `lake_mod`, predict the nose color for a 15 year old lion and the freeze duration for a future winter.

```{r}
predict(lion_mod, newdata = tibble(age = 15))

0.07 + 0.059*15
```

```{r}
predict(lake_mod, newdata = tibble(year1 = 3000))
```




# Prediction intervals

We can use `predict` to provide either a point estimate or an interval estimate.  A confidence interval gives the average nose color for all 5 year old lions, i.e. the height of the line.  The default behavior is to build a 95% CI.

```{r}
predict(lion_mod, newdata = tibble(age = 5))

predict(lion_mod, newdata = tibble(age = 5), interval = "confidence",
        level = 0.95)
```

How certain are we that the line was drawn in the right place, based on our data? Let's make a bunch of CIs.

```{r}
predict(lion_mod, newdata = tibble(age = 1:10))

lion_CIs <- predict(lion_mod, newdata = tibble(age = 1:13),
               interval = "confidence")

lion_CIs
```

This is what the gray ribbon in `geom_smooth()` is doing!

```{r}
ggplot(lions, aes(age, black)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  geom_line(data = as_tibble(lion_CIs),
            mapping = aes(x = 1:13, y = lwr), color = "forestgreen") +
  geom_line(data = as_tibble(lion_CIs),
            mapping = aes(x = 1:13, y = upr), color = "forestgreen") +
  labs(
    title = "Lion Ages vs. % nose black",
    subtitle = "With Confidence Regression Interval in Green"
  )  +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 20),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 15))
```


The estimated nose color for a single 5 year old lion is given by a prediction interval.  This is wider than a CI.

```{r}
predict(lion_mod, newdata = tibble(age = 5), interval = "confidence")
predict(lion_mod, newdata = tibble(age = 5), interval = "prediction")
```


In a scatterplot, the lines formed by the PIs contain approximately 95% of the points.

```{r}
lion_PIs <- predict(lion_mod, newdata = tibble(age = 1:13),
               interval = "prediction")

ggplot(lions, aes(age, black)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(data = as_tibble(lion_PIs), mapping = aes(x = 1:13, y = lwr)) +
  geom_line(data = as_tibble(lion_PIs), mapping = aes(x = 1:13, y = upr)) +
  labs(
    title = "Lion Ages vs. % nose black",
    subtitle = "With Prediction Intervals"
  ) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 20),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 15))
```


We can build these intervals by hand using the "Residual standard error", $s$, extracted from the summary output with `sigma`.

```{r}
summary(lion_mod)

summary(lion_mod)$sigma

n <- nrow(lions)
```

The null distribution is a T with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.

```{r}
pt_est <- predict(lion_mod, newdata = tibble(age = 5))

s <- summary(lion_mod)$sigma
se <- s*sqrt( 1/n + (5 - mean(lions$age))^2 / ((n-1)*var(lions$age)) )

cv <- qt(0.975, df = n-2)

c(pt_est - cv*se, pt_est + cv*se)
```

```{r}
predict(lion_mod, newdata = tibble(age = 5), interval = "confidence")
```


We can also recreate the prediction interval by hand by adding a +1 term in the square root in the SE calculation.

```{r}
pt_est <- predict(lion_mod, newdata = tibble(age = 5))

s <- summary(lion_mod)$sigma
se <- s*sqrt(1 + 1/n + (5 - mean(lions$age))^2 / ((n-1)*var(lions$age)) )

cv <- qt(0.975, df = n-2)

c(pt_est - cv*se, pt_est + cv*se)
```

```{r}
predict(lion_mod, newdata = tibble(age = 5), interval = "prediction")
```
